entry.title: How to save website form data
entry.summary: How to save entered form data on a website
entry.content:
I want it to be simple

Continuing in my pattern of attempting things that seem simple at first, but turn into a rabbit hole. I was filling out a (single page) web form that was quite long and I needed to pause my progress, I wanted to capture my responses so that if accidently closed the page, I didn't lose my responses. Also I thought it would be good forward planning to keep a copy of my responses myself.

Of course, it is possible to copy and paste each response individually, but this is exactly the sort of repetitive toil I try to excise from my life.

The Initial Attempt

Sometimes the simplest solution works so we will try it. To select all page elements, the shortcut Ctrl+A works in many circumstances. Using the shortcut on our completed form, we want to see whether the input is also selected.

Unfortunately, this approach doesn't work as it only selects elements of the form itself and doesn't include my responses.

Autofilled forms?

Firefox and Chrome support autofill of forms for certain fields of the form which is great for repeated entry of your address etc. This usage is slightly different than what I wanted because I want to save all fields in a given form I am currently filling out, including fields that have never been seen before.

Extensions?

There are extensions which improve the experience of filling in longer forms, the main one I am aware of is Form History Control.

Copying the HTML

Let us look at the options for us built-in to the browser. These options both use the Developer Tools.

After I thought about why this happening, it made sense to me pretty quickly that copying the HTML markup was not going to return my responses. HTML is a markup language which defines the structure of webpages, it really doesn't concern itself with the interactivity of the webpage when it is being displayed by the web browser. We need to find a way to access the document as it is being presented by the browser.

Accessing the DOM

We can also access the DOM (Document Object Model) using the Developer Tools. It is an interface that lends itself to accessing the data of the objects that are present in the webpage as it being displayed. I created a small Javascript snippet that returns the contents of all input fields of selected element kinds.

  • <input> elements need to be selected as most user input occurs in them
  • <textarea> elements can be writable so we should grab their contents
  • <select> elements need to be included as dropdown selections use them
const formFields = document.querySelectorAll('input, textarea, select');
const fieldData = [];
formFields.forEach(field => {
  fieldData.push({
    name: field.name,
    value: field.value,
    autoname: field.attributes['autocomplete']
    });
});
var newWindow = window.open();
const formatted = fieldData.map(obj => JSON.stringify(obj)).join('\n');
newWindow.document.write('<pre>' + formatted + '</pre>'); })();

I have tested this code snippets with standard HTML forms as , then I tested it with some forms created in Google Forms as that is very popular. The form that trigger this inquiry was actually created by Cognito, I hadn't heard about this company before. It presented some problems with my first attempt at this code; the name attribute of the final output objects were not defined. I eventually found that there is an autocomplete attribute that contained the name of the given field so I simply included that in the dump as well.

Now we have Javascript code that accesses the DOM to get the content of input fields in a good variety of cases, how do we package it for easy usage?

Bookmarklets

A bookmarklet is a Javascript script that can run on click, similar to how a normal bookmark will trigger the browser to load the linked website.

Overall, it is a great idea. Once I have my code snippet inside the URI for the bookmarklet, it will open a new window with the list of objects (map containing the name, value and autocomplete) of the selected fields printed. The only thing I can complain about is that the entry for the bookmark URI is not designed to handle multiline input (because most bookmarket targets are usually a single line URL of course) so the developer UX leaves a lot to be desired.

Conclusion

Although, I could definitely improve the accessibility of using my bookmarklet (the output format of the form response dump is a bit ugly), I decided I was happy enough with the outcome of this exercise. I now get a simple dump of the name of the input elements along with their contents.

Some improvements I could envision myself making:

  • Iterating over the document top to bottom, dumping all HTML content alongside the field contents
  • Pretty printing the field data objects
  • Adding more metadata in the field data objects .eg types

entry.title: How to install all my GOG games
entry.summary: A journey to bulk install some games
entry.content:
Subject Matter

Steam and GOG (Good Old Games) are online stores for purchasing video games which can be downloaded (it all happens digitally these days).

I recently purchased an excess of storage for my main computer (four 2TB SSDs) and wanted to make use of it by installing a good chunk of the games from my Steam library. When the Library tab of the Steam client is selected, your list of games is presented by name and small icon on the left side. Selecting games in bulk is easily achieved by holding the Shift key and selecting each game on the list, then you can right click on a selected item to bring up a context menu including actions to perform in bulk (installation being one of them).

Furthermore, games can be easily sorted into categories. Overall, the user experience was very pleasant and I had setup the queue of games to be installed very quickly. Even with so much storage, I had to be selective about which Steam games I installed (Steam sales are my weakness). I don't need to be so cautious with my collection of GOG games as there are less of them and they don't use as much storage per game. I aimed to install all of my GOG games on a single 2TB drive, I felt this should be a simple task.

Problem

Similarly to how Steam provides a client to install and manage your game collection, GOG has provided their own client. It is called GOG Galaxy and it looks pretty slick with a polished purple aesthetic. By default, the games are presented visually as rows of products on shelves but this can be changed to a more traditional list view which I prefer.

Unfortunately, I discovered there is no way to select games in bulk in the GOG Galaxy client. If I wanted to install all my games, I would need to click the install button on each game entry, then click again in each dialog to confirm the installation. This would result in hundreds of mouse clicks when really I wanted a single mouse click to install ALL games, this possibility was not even present with my Steam bulk installation as I couldn't install each and every game.

After determining that this feature is not present in the GOG Galaxy client, I decided to explore other possibilities.

Direct Downloads

Galaxy was not always provided by GOG and before it existed, the way to download and manage your games was on the GOG website. You can download the installers from here and run them on your computer. Someone has built a python script to bulk download direct installers and additional content from the GOG website, which would probably be the best option for what I want.

The reason I didn't go with this option is because I stubbornly wanted to install the games with GOG Galaxy integration.

Alternate Clients

GOG Galaxy does not have native Linux support. If you want to manage your GOG games on a Linux system, your best bet is to use Lutris. My main computer is running Windows 10 and there are alternative game launcher clients that run on Windows: Heroic and Playnite.

I thought maybe one of these alternative clients might support bulk installation but unfortunately even though they let you select multiple games simultaneously they don't let you install them in bulk. I started to consider making changes to these launchers to add this feature as they are both open source but the thought of learning a new codebase I am unfamiliar with is daunting. There had to be an easier way.

Automation the Lazy Way

I decided to use AutoHotkey in order to automate the process. Using Playnite, I connected it to my GOG account and it downloaded all the metadata for my games. Then it presented me the list of all my GOG games, with which I could craft a script to repeatedly press down and enter to start installing each game.

#Persistent
SetTimer, PressKeys, 1000
return

PressKeys:
Send, {Down}
Sleep, 100
Send, {Enter}
return

Esc::ExitApp

That last line is very important as it allows me to cease the script once it has reached the bottom of the list by pressing the Escape key. Not quite pressing a single button, but once you set it up and run it, it will work for any number of games. At least that is what I hoped...

Performance Issues

Once the game has been selected in Playnite, it does eventually appear in the GOG Galaxy download queue exactly as I intended. The problem is that when the download queue started to expand to a size of about 300, the client really started to struggle.

The client would take a long time to even show the Downloads entry in the menu upon starting up. It is hard to say why the program struggled so much without having access to the source code, however I rummaged around in the configuration files to see if there was some clues. I figured out that the client uses sqlite to store its job queue. It is not encrypted and can be explored easily using a tool like DB Browser. Sometimes the stalls could be fixed by clearing the job queue (there is a jobs table that can be cleared with a simple SQL TRUNCATE statement) or even deleting the jobs database file completely, but mostly it was a waiting game.

Another problem is that some installers that run through the GOG Galaxy are not fully quiet and require user interaction in order to continue so I needed to check it regularly.

After a long wait over 4 days, checking and restarting the GOG Galaxy client each time it stalled. I eventually installed every GOG game. After trimming down and removing some duplicate games I ended up with 492 installed GOG games which took up 845 GB on my drive.

Conclusion

Ultimately, I achieved the outcome that I wanted although it was far more time consuming than I expected it to be. I went down some rabbit holes but found a solution that is reasonably simple but flawed. As of the time of writing, Steam really is the most featureful client out of any proprietary game launcher and that is no doubt playing massively into its success. I have found that other game launchers are missing features I expect as standard because they are present in Steam, fortunately there are open source game launchers that the community could rally around to reach parity with Steam.
